title: Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial
author: Ethan Goh · Robert Gallo · Jason Hom · Eric Strong · Yingjie Weng · Hannah Kerman · Joséphine A. Cool · Zahir Kanjee · Andrew S. Parsons · Neera Ahuja · Eric Horvitz · Daniel Yang · Arnold Milstein · Andrew P. J. Olson · Adam Rodman · Jonathan H. Chen

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of jagged, task-specific capability and materially strengthens it with randomized evidence from clinical reasoning: standalone model performance did not translate into better human–AI performance through access alone. It identifies interaction design, prompting, training, workflow integration and realistic use-context evaluation as necessary complements, while retaining physician oversight rather than endorsing autonomy.
qs: These results suggest that access alone to LLMs will not improve overall physician diagnostic reasoning in practice.

The LLM alone outperformed physicians even when the LLM was available to them, indicating that further development in human-computer interactions is needed to realize the potential of AI in clinical decision support systems.

st.t: Clinical support: Practitioner gains may not help patients
st.an: The source is consistent with the cluster’s qualified framing: it identifies a simulated-patient trial reporting improved GP diagnostic accuracy but supplies no evidence of patient outcomes, routine-care benefits, workflow effects or workforce consequences. Its other citations identify research questions and topics rather than results, reinforcing the cluster’s caution against broader conclusions.
qs: Early diagnostic suggestions improve accuracy of GPs: a randomised controlled trial using computer-simulated patients.
Should electronic differential diagnosis support be used early or late in the diagnostic process?

kp.k: Trial tested physician augmentation rather than autonomous clinical practice
kp.d: This medical study, published October 28, 2024, randomized 50 US-licensed physicians to ChatGPT Plus (GPT-4) plus conventional resources or conventional resources alone, with 25 per group and stratification by career stage. Conducted November 29–December 29, 2023, it included 26 attendings and 24 residents; 44 participants trained in internal medicine, 5 in emergency medicine and 1 in family medicine. Participants had 60 minutes to complete up to 6 clinical vignettes. Analyses followed intention-to-treat principles, using blinded grading and models accounting for participant and case variability.
qs: We performed a randomized clinical trial to compare the diagnostic reasoning performance of physicians using a commercial LLM AI chatbot (ChatGPT Plus [GPT-4]; OpenAI) compared with conventional diagnostic resources (eg, UpToDate, Google).
Participants were randomized to either access the LLM in addition to conventional diagnostic resources or conventional resources only, stratified by career stage.
All analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle and were conducted at the case level, clustered by the participant.

kp.k: LLM access did not significantly improve physician reasoning
kp.d: Physicians completed 244 cases: 125 in the LLM group and 119 in the control group. Median diagnostic reasoning scores were 76% (IQR, 66%-87%) with LLM access and 74% (IQR, 63%-84%) with conventional resources. The adjusted difference was 2 percentage points (95% CI, −4 to 8; P = .60). Including incomplete cases produced a similar result. The authors report qualitatively similar findings across career-stage and prior-LLM-experience subgroups, concluding that access alone did not deliver improved diagnostic reasoning under these conditions.
qs: A total of 244 cases were completed by all participants (125 cases in LLM group, 119 cases in control group).
The median score per case was 76% (IQR, 66%-87%) for the LLM group and 74% (IQR, 63%-84%) for the control group.
These results suggest that access alone to LLMs will not improve overall physician diagnostic reasoning in practice.

kp.k: Time savings and diagnostic accuracy improvements remained unconfirmed
kp.d: Median time per case was 519 seconds (IQR, 371-668) with LLM access versus 565 (IQR, 456-788) in controls; the adjusted difference was −82 seconds (95% CI, −195 to 31). The abstract and results narrative report P = .20, whereas Table 3 reports .15; neither indicates statistical significance. Final-diagnosis results were also nonsignificant: ordinal odds ratio 1.4 (95% CI, 0.7-2.8; P = .39) and binary odds ratio 1.9 (95% CI, 0.9-4.0; P = .10). The authors call for substantially larger studies to evaluate time differences given wide variability.
qs: Our data did not confirm any differences in time spent solving cases.

With wide variability observed in time to complete cases, future studies with substantially larger sample sizes would be necessary to evaluate whether physicians with experience using LLMs spend less time on diagnostic reasoning.
In assessing the accuracy of final diagnoses, treating them as binary (correct vs incorrect) variables did not qualitatively change the results (odds ratio, 1.9; 95% CI, 0.9-4.0; *P* = .10).

kp.k: Standalone LLM achieved higher scores in exploratory comparison
kp.d: Across 3 standalone runs, the LLM's median rubric score was 92% (IQR, 82%-97%). Compared with conventional-resource physicians, the adjusted difference was 16 percentage points (95% CI, 2-30; P = .03). The authors describe standalone performance as exceeding both physician groups. This was a secondary exploratory comparison, not the randomized intervention: researchers iteratively developed a standardized zero-shot prompt, ran it in separate sessions and submitted unchanged responses for blinded grading. Secondary analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
qs: In the 3 runs of the LLM alone, the median score per case was 92% (IQR, 82%-97%).
Comparing LLM alone with the control group found an absolute score difference of 16 percentage points (95% CI, 2-30 percentage points; *P* = .03) favoring the LLM alone.
The researcher physician inputting prompts to the model did not alter model responses.
Analysis of the secondary outcomes was exploratory without adjusting for multiple comparisons.

kp.k: Prompting and workflow design are proposed collaboration mechanisms
kp.d: The authors suggest that sensitivity to prompt formulation may explain the standalone model's stronger performance; this explanation was not established by the trial. They propose clinician training in prompting, predefined prompts integrated into documentation and workflows, and interactions that identify clinical features inconsistent with a proposed differential diagnosis. These are recommendations for improving human–AI collaboration, not tested interventions or demonstrated benefits.
qs: This may be explained by the sensitivity of LLM output to prompt formulation.
Training clinicians in best prompting practices may improve physician performance with LLMs.

Alternatively, organizations could invest in predefined prompting for diagnostic decision support integrated into clinical workflows and documentation, enabling synergy between the tools and clinicians.

kp.k: Untrained, discretionary use reflected current chatbot deployment
kp.d: Physicians received chatbot access without explicit prompt-engineering training and were not required to interact with it consistently. The authors deliberately chose this design to approximate effectiveness in current deployments, noting that health systems often provide compliant chatbots with minimal training. All 22 available intervention transcripts showed LLM use; 3 transcripts were lost to technical issues. The trial therefore examined access under discretionary use, rather than a standardized, trained collaboration protocol.
qs: Participants were given access to the chatbot without explicit training in prompt engineering techniques that could have improved the quality of their interactions with the system; however, this is consistent with current integrations and thus requires this representative evaluation.
Furthermore, even though all of the physicians in the LLM arm at least tried to use the system based on chat logs, they were not forced to use the system in any consistent way.
This was a purposeful design to better reflect an effectiveness evaluation in the clinical practice setting.

kp.k: Assessment measured reasoning processes beyond final-answer accuracy
kp.d: The study adapted structured reflection to score differential diagnoses, supporting and opposing findings, final diagnosis and next diagnostic steps. Appropriate reasoning from an incorrect differential diagnosis was not penalized. Rubrics were refined through 65 pilot cases completed by 13 participants excluded from the final trial. Each trial case was independently assessed by 2 blinded scorers, with consensus discussions for differences exceeding 10% of the final score. Weighted Cohen κ was 0.66 and Cronbach α was 0.64, increasing to 0.67 after removing final diagnosis. The authors present this as a richer evaluation framework than multiple-choice benchmarks.
qs: We built on previous studies of structured reflection by scoring the grid itself, not just final diagnosis accuracy.
While incorrect differential diagnoses were not awarded points, appropriate reasoning based on those diagnoses were not penalized.
The weighted Cohen κ value between all 3 graders was 0.66, indicating substantial agreement within the expected range for diagnostic performance studies.
The overall Cronbach α value was 0.64.

kp.k: Higher vignette scores do not justify autonomous diagnosis
kp.d: The authors explicitly reject interpreting standalone performance as support for diagnosis without physician oversight. Clinicians had already curated and summarized the cases, excluding patient interviewing, data collection and contextual understanding from the tested task. Rubric improvements were treated as a signal of reasoning performance, not evidence of better patient outcomes; broader clinical trials are needed to establish downstream clinical impact.
qs: Results of this study should not be interpreted to indicate that LLMs should be used for diagnosis autonomously without physician oversight.

The clinical case vignettes were curated and summarized by human clinicians, a pragmatic and common approach to isolate the diagnostic reasoning process, but this does not capture competence in many other areas important to clinical reasoning, including patient interviewing and data collection.

Additionally, improvement in rubric scoring here represents an important signal of clinical reasoning, but broader clinical trials are necessary to assess for meaningful differences in downstream clinical impact.

kp.k: Single-model, six-case design limits breadth of findings
kp.d: The trial evaluated one commercially available LLM and 6 cases chosen for a broad range of pathology while avoiding simplistic and exceedingly rare presentations. Cases derived from actual patients and included initial-evaluation information; the authors state that the unreleased cases were excluded from LLM training data. They acknowledge that this sample cannot cover medicine comprehensively and was intended to assess general reasoning across selected cases rather than comprehensive individual knowledge.
qs: We focused our investigation around a single LLM, given its commercial availability and integration into clinical practice.
The cases have never been publicly released to protect the validity of the test materials for future use, and therefore are excluded from training data of the LLM.
No sample of clinical vignettes can comprehensively cover the variety of cases in the field of medicine.
This is not meant to comprehensively assess a participant’s knowledge, but rather to evaluate their general clinical reasoning across a set of cases.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Goh and coauthors report that access to GPT-4 did not significantly improve physicians’ diagnostic reasoning, although the standalone model scored higher. They propose training and workflow redesign as possible routes to better collaboration, not demonstrated improvements.
pts.d: The claims concern medicine, not legal services. Physicians with access to ChatGPT Plus and conventional resources had a median diagnostic reasoning score of 76%, versus 74% with conventional resources alone; the adjusted difference was 2 percentage points (95% CI, −4 to 8; P = .60). Neither case-completion time nor final diagnosis accuracy showed statistically significant improvements. The standalone LLM achieved a median rubric score of 92%, and the authors describe it as outperforming both physician groups. They suggest that prompting practices may explain this gap and that clinician training, predefined prompts integrated into clinical workflows, and interactions that highlight contradictory clinical features might improve collaboration. These explanations and proposed interventions were not established by the trial.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a randomized, single-blind vignette trial involving 50 physicians; standalone model performance was a secondary exploratory comparison.
pts.d: Twenty-five physicians were assigned to each arm, stratified by career stage. Participants completed 244 case responses across six selected clinical vignettes. The primary outcome used an adapted structured-reflection rubric covering differential diagnoses, supporting and opposing findings, final diagnosis, and next diagnostic steps, with blinded physician grading and consensus procedures. Analyses followed intention-to-treat and accounted for participant and case clustering. The standalone model answered each case across three separate runs using an iteratively developed zero-shot prompt, with responses unchanged by the researcher and graded blind alongside human responses. Its adjusted advantage over the conventional-resources group was 16 percentage points (95% CI, 2–30; P = .03). Secondary analyses were exploratory and not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The proposed benefits of prompting training and workflow integration draw on interpretation of these results and cited literature rather than a tested intervention. For timing, the abstract and narrative report P = .20, whereas Table 3 reports .15; both indicate a nonsignificant result.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings describe GPT-4 use in a one-hour vignette exercise conducted in late 2023, without explicit prompting training; they do not establish autonomous diagnostic competence or downstream patient benefit.
pts.d: The trial ran from November 29 to December 29, 2023, and was published October 28, 2024. Physicians had 60 minutes to complete up to six cases and could use conventional resources in either arm. The intervention provided chatbot access without explicit prompt-engineering training or a standardized manner of use. Only one LLM was studied. Cases were curated and summarized by clinicians, so the exercise did not assess patient interviewing, data collection, or contextual clinical judgment. The authors explicitly reject interpreting standalone model performance as support for diagnosis without physician oversight and call for broader clinical trials to establish downstream impact. Future improvements through training and integration have no specified delivery date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The implications concern physicians, health systems deploying chatbots, medical educators, and ultimately patients; the study does not make workforce-displacement or legal-market claims.
pts.d: Participants were 26 attending physicians and 24 residents recruited through three US academic medical institutions. Most were trained in internal medicine (44 of 50), with five in emergency medicine and one in family medicine. Results were qualitatively similar across training-level and prior-chatbot-experience subgroups. For physicians, chatbot availability alone did not yield a demonstrated diagnostic performance gain under the tested conditions. For health systems and educators, the authors identify a need to develop workforce skills and human-computer interactions rather than rely on access alone. Patients are potential downstream beneficiaries of improved decision support, but clinical outcomes were not measured and the authors retain physician oversight as essential.
